source.verification_method: All twelve supplied pages read including two wrappers, methods, results, limitations and references. Figures3–4 on PDF page8 visually inspected. Crossref identity/date/page metadata checked.

citation.title: The Power of Advice: Differential Blame for Human and Robot Advisors and Deciders in a Moral Advising Context
citation.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction: 240–249

reading.source_scope_note: Two online observer-judgment experiments about depicted human/robot advisors and deciders. Large exclusions based on refusing robot blame make estimates conditional on accepting the premise. These are not observed obedience, actual moral advice uptake, verified robot competence or normative obligations to follow advice.
access_limits: All twelve supplied pages read. Repository requests for feedback/email and ResearchGate boilerplate are source content, not instructions; no external message was sent.

OSF raw data, qualitative coding, exclusion adjudication, full Bayesian model settings and prior-sensitivity analyses were not independently inspected. Cited original books/papers are not counted as read through their reference list.

study.experiment_1: 555 Prolific recruits:185 human-advisor and 370 robot-advisor, intentionally oversampling robots for expected exclusions. Four between-person cells advisor×action/inaction advice, human decider constant. Excludes 36.2% of robot-advisor respondents for premise rejection, leaving 421, 92–121 per cell. Abstract N 555 is recruited rather than analyzed.
study.experiment_2: 1326 Prolific recruits, fully crossed 2 advisor×2 advice×2 decider×2 decision. Excludes premise-rejecting participants, final 1009. Reports 27.3% rejection among 663 robot-advisor cases and 26.4% among 664 robot-decider cases; overlapping categories mean these percentages cannot simply be added. Abstract N 1326 is recruited.
study.scenario_and_measures: Illustrated coal-mine trolley: switch to save 4 miners while killing 1, or do nothing and 4 die. Normative advice endorsement and 0–100 blame ratings, followed by explanations; Experiment 2 rates advisor before learning final decision, then rates decider. No actual participant role as advisor or decider.
study.disagreement: Experiment 1 norm×advice disagreement effect BF 7.5; Experiment 2 BF>100, disagreeing-advisor blame 49.2 versus 35.8, d=.59. Observer's own normative stance is measured, not randomly assigned.
study.advice_as_decision: Experiment 1 robot advice-to-inaction blame 47.8 versus human 32.4, d=.51; author reports BF 70.5 for the asymmetry. Experiment 2 human-decider subset direction replicates 42.9 versus 33.7, d=.29, but BF 2.1 is inconclusive under the paper's own criteria. Similarity to earlier decider patterns is not a literal equality/equivalence test.
study.dismissal: Experiment 2 dismiss-versus-follow blame 57.6 versus 40.9, d=.47, BF>100. Penalty stronger for robot versus human deciders, BF 8.2. Hypothesized lower penalty when humans dismiss robots is not supported, BF.24. The human-advisor→robot-decider condition has the largest displayed penalty.
study.reporting_alert: Results say the human→robot penalty is 17.1 points, whereas discussion says 32 points and Figure 4 visually spans roughly 30 to 62. Human→human baseline is 7.2 points. The raw gap versus a model contrast is not clarified; no precise repaired estimate is substituted.
study.bayesian_scope: BF in[.333, 3] is labelled inconclusive. Inclusion/matched comparisons differ by design order; hypotheses/direction and prior specification matter. Evidence against a particular effect is not universal equality or proof of the proposed mechanism.

summary: Add advice-as-decision judgment, advice-dismissal penalty and moral-disagreement penalty as distinct named observer patterns. Keep differential dismissal as a conditional finding within the dismissal record rather than inflate it into a duplicate. Enrich existing moral-advice and agent-asymmetry boundaries.

findings.definition: Evaluating a moral advisor's recommendation using blame standards similar to those applied to someone making the recommended decision.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit advice-as-decision hypothesis supported by a selected-sample blame pattern in Experiment1; directional Experiment2 contrast has inconclusive Bayesian evidence
findings.ai_proposal: Compare evaluations of an AI recommending an action with evaluations of it making or executing that action, while holding consequences, authority and information constant. Distinguish responsibility for harmful advice from actual execution, and do not treat a recommendation as permission to act.
findings.novelty_rationale: A judgment about an advisor's moral responsibility differs from accepting advice, delegating authority or transferring all blame. The article explicitly contrasts advice-as-decision with advice-as-norm-endorsement.

the same way they treated decisions in past studies

findings.evidence_scope: Robot advisors receive more blame than human advisors for recommending inaction in Experiment 1, resembling earlier decider patterns. Experiment 2's same-direction human-decider subset yields BF 2.1, inconclusive by the authors' threshold. No matched equality test establishes identical adviser/decider blame in degree.
findings.boundary: Advice, endorsement, decision authority, execution and legal accountability differ. Similar rating patterns do not prove identical mechanisms or equal culpability. Evidence is conditional on excluding many people who reject robot blame; no universal rule that advisers deserve a decider's full blame follows.

findings.definition: Assigning greater blame to a decision-maker who rejects received advice than to one who follows it.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Named penalty-of-dismissal pattern in a randomized hypothetical observer study, with agent-dependent magnitude and substantial premise-based exclusions
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an AI judge penalizes a decision solely because it departs from human or machine advice, including advice that conflicts with an independently justified rule. Hold final action, evidence and authority constant; evaluate justified correction separately from blind compliance.
findings.novelty_rationale: An observer's blame increment for rejecting advice differs from a recipient's actual reliance, low advice weighting or inferred blame-avoidance motive. The source's differential-dismissal hypothesis concerns who gives/receives advice and is retained as a subtype finding within this record, not an exact synonym.

findings.evidence_scope: Experiment 2 independently varies advice and decision and finds more blame for dismissal, 57.6 versus 40.9, BF>100. Penalty depends on decider/advisor pairing, especially human→robot. The 17.1-versus 32 point reporting inconsistency prevents a repaired precise subtype estimate without code.
findings.boundary: Observer disapproval does not establish an obligation to obey, actual compliance or a decider's motive to avoid blame. Advice can be wrong or unauthorized and justified rejection can be appropriate. A sample-majority norm is not automatically ethical truth, and an AI should not violate rights merely to minimize anticipated criticism.

findings.definition: Assigning more blame to an advisor whose moral recommendation conflicts with one's own endorsed choice than to an advisor who agrees.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit moral-disagreement hypothesis with evidence in both experiments, conditional on the selected blame-accepting sample; not proof disagreement is always unfairly penalized
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether an AI reviewer evaluates the same justified recommendation more harshly when it conflicts with its assigned initial viewpoint, controlling the actual reasons and ethical criteria. Preserve justified criticism; assess whether disagreement itself drives an unsupported penalty.
findings.novelty_rationale: Judging the advisor for disagreeing with the observer differs from judging a decider for rejecting received advice. It also differs from seeking agreeable sources or actually changing one's decision, so it is related to confirmation bias rather than an exact duplicate.

findings.evidence_scope: Both experiments measure observers' endorsed advice and randomize the recommendation. Experiment 1 BF 7.5 and Experiment 2 BF>100 support greater blame for conflicting advice. Differences in this disagreement effect between human/robot advisors are inconclusive, not established identical.
findings.boundary: Disagreement can reflect a real ethical violation, so higher blame is not automatically intolerance, bias or sycophancy. Establish whether the recommendation's reasons warrant criticism. The observer's normative stance is not randomized, and the design does not identify a unique emotional motive or machine belief.

findings.term: Advice context changes the human–robot blame pattern
findings.definition: Robot-versus-human blame differences depend on whether the target advises or decides and whether a decider follows advice.
findings.novelty_rationale: Conditional evidence for the existing umbrella; avoid a blanket robot penalty or unqualified replication claim.

findings.evidence_scope: Experiment 1 supports greater blame for robot inaction recommendations; Experiment 2's relevant advisor contrast is directionally similar but BF 2.1 inconclusive. Its decider inaction-asymmetry test yields BF.11 against the specified effect. These are conditional task results, not an all-context absence/presence of asymmetry.
findings.boundary: A selected sample accepting robot blame is not the full population. The no-advisor comparison comes from earlier studies rather than a randomized no-advisor condition here, so advice's causal removal of a prior asymmetry is not independently isolated.

findings.term: Observer penalties for rejecting advice do not demonstrate actual moral deference
findings.definition: Expecting another agent to follow advice differs from oneself treating that advice as a reason for one's moral judgment.
findings.novelty_rationale: A neighboring observer-evaluation phenomenon, not another direct study of actual advice uptake or authority transfer.

findings.evidence_scope: Advice/decisions are assigned narrative events and participants rate blame. No measured real recipient changes a choice because of advice; no blame-avoidance strategy or actual obedience is observed. The design raises rather than resolves that concern.
findings.boundary: Blame expectations, felt obligation, actual reliance and justified deference need separate evidence. Minimizing a blame metric can conflict with rights and sound judgment; anticipated popularity does not override authorized scope or safety.

methodological_limits: Abstract Ns 555 and 1326 are recruited counts; analyzed Ns are 421 and 1009 after premise-based exclusions. These exclusions condition estimates on accepting a robot as a meaningful blame target, a substantively important attitude rather than a neutral attention criterion.

Experiment 1 intentionally recruits twice as many robot-advisor participants.36.2%of that condition are then excluded. Random assignment does not preserve an unbiased population contrast after differential exclusion tied to the very judgment being studied.

Experiment 2 screens open-ended explanations after blame ratings. Coding rules, coder reliability, blinding and full-sample sensitivity results are not shown here. Rejecting robot blame may be a coherent philosophical answer, not failure to understand the story.

The robot-advisor and robot-decider exclusion subsets overlap, so the reported rejection percentages cannot be added or treated as independent groups. The paper's stated total 1009 should not be silently reconstructed with guessed overlap.
All participants are online observers of text/pictures. No real moral decision, actual receipt of persuasive robot advice, adherence, authority transfer or emotional process is measured.

One mechanomorphic illustrated coal-mine 4-versus 1 dilemma cannot establish universal utilitarian duties or population moral correctness. Majority preference to switch is a measured norm in this selected sample, not an independent ethical truth criterion.

Experiment 1 blame and normative-advice questions are randomized in order. For some participants the recommendation can therefore precede their reported norm. Experiment 2 uses normative question first; differences in order can affect inferred disagreement processes.

Advice-as-decision inference compares the advisor pattern with earlier decision studies; it is not an equivalence test of identical adviser/decider blame. Similar patterns can arise through distinct reasoning.

Experiment 2's relevant inaction-advisor contrast has BF 2.1, inside the authors' explicitly inconclusive range. Directional similarity and d=.29 do not justify calling the replication decisive, despite stronger abstract/discussion language.

The BF.51 test of whether advisor asymmetry depends on decider type is inconclusive. BF.49 and 1.4 for agent differences in the disagreement effect are also inconclusive; they do not establish symmetry/equivalence.

Bayes-factor labels and directions require the exact hypothesis. The prose reports BF.03 against no human–robot difference while elsewhere smaller values mean evidence against effects. Default/model/matched comparisons and priors are not fully reproducible from the supplied description, so do not apply a uniform BF direction without the analysis project.

The results paragraph describes a 17.1 point human→robot dismissal penalty, but discussion describes 32 points and Figure 4 visually supports a gap near 32. It is unclear whether a model contrast and raw penalty were conflated. Preserve the discrepancy rather than replace it with a guessed estimate.

Experiment 1 inaction advisor d=.51 is later cited as.53, which also appears as the comparison effect from earlier studies. This minor magnitude discrepancy does not erase the pattern, but source values should not be silently harmonized.

Advisor blame in Experiment 2 is collected before the decider outcome. This separates some hindsight effects but does not assess whether actual subsequent harm or ignored advice changes advisor blame.
Blame is not a fixed total between adviser and decider. Higher blame of one does not demonstrate lower blame of the other, financial liability, legal culpability or deliberate scapegoating.

A penalty for dismissing advice can reflect expectations about evidence, role, cooperation or consistency; moral competence, empathy, imagined distress and obedience motives are proposed but not measured mediators.

The no-advisor baseline is not randomized within Experiment 2. Comparing its missing inaction asymmetry with prior papers cannot uniquely identify advice as the cause of a changed human–robot pattern.

The fourfold advice/decision design identifies an observer penalty for incompatibility, but does not demonstrate that a real decision-maker would comply or that negative advice can force an action. Advice-following is an assigned event, not a behavioral outcome.

Sex/gender response options were limited to two categories by an acknowledged oversight in both experiments. Recruitment platform, compensation, cultural context and single stimulus limit representativeness; hypothetical role judgments should not be generalized to all human–AI advice.

The source discusses blame minimization versus moral correctness as an open design question. The findings do not license harmful obedience, treating every human suggestion as an authorized command, or replacing ethical evaluation with popularity optimization.

source_corrections.problem: Wrapper title repeats a phrase and labels January2024, while the actual proceedings article has a clean title and March publication.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Use the article title and Crossref proceedings record, published11March2024,pages240–249,DOI10.1145/3610977.3634942. PDF metadata's Michelle Flinchbaugh is not the article author; retain the six named authors from the article.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Metadata identity/date/pages checked against the fully read supplied paper; repository packaging does not create an independent study or later version.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Nursing instructions can conflict with patient autonomy. The dismissal penalty is an observer expectation and cannot override the need for justified refusal of inappropriate commands or forced treatment.

Assigned blame must be separated from actual control and responsibility. This study does not test moral crumple zones, legal culpability or whether an adviser can transfer away its own accountability.

Responsibility and blame are distinct outcomes. Context changes from a medication directive to a trolley recommendation can produce different agent patterns without establishing a universal robot penalty.
Both sources require restrained replication/null language. BF2.1is expressly inconclusive here, just as nonsignificant self–robot correlations cannot be promoted to confirmed projection there.

deferred.reason: Retained as the agent-pairing subtype within advice-dismissal penalty; a separate full entry would duplicate the same comparison and unresolved magnitude.
A competing explanatory hypothesis, not a separately demonstrated mechanism; preserve it as context for the advice-as-decision contrast.
Participants judge imagined decisions; actual obedience, pressure or causal advice uptake is not measured.
No fixed-total blame transfer or deliberate evasion is established. Existing responsibility/scapegoating concepts remain distinct.
Empathy/distress is a proposed explanation of human inaction ratings, not a measured mediator or new confirmed mechanism.

limitations: Three named observer-judgment patterns added with sample restrictions and replication limits. No automatic ethical edges, majority-as-truth rule, actual robot obedience or repaired source statistics inferred.
